It has been a privilege to represent the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group and to be able to guide them through this case. Understandably, it is with very mixed feelings that the group makes an affirmative recommendation of any route anywhere in the study area. But barring legislative intervention, the application will move forward. Based on the evidence presented and the applicable criteria for review of the same, Route 894 best meets the routing criteria governing this proceeding.

5. Route 
The Commission must determine which route best satisfies the routing criteria established by statute and rule.
The Commission must determine which route best satisfies the routing criteria established by statute and rule.
Under PURA § 37.056(c), the Commission must consider several factors when evaluating transmission line routes, including community values, recreational and park areas, historic and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of costs to consumers. 
The Commission's routing rule, 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B), further provides that transmission lines should be routed to moderate impacts on the affected community and landowners to the extent reasonable, while considering engineering constraints and costs. 
In applying these standards, objective routing metrics such as cost, route length, the number of habitable structures affected, compatibility with existing land uses, and engineering feasibility are evaluated. The Commission selects the route that best meets the routing criteria when all factors are considered together.

A.	Statutory Criteria under PURA § 37.056(c)(4) compel the selection of Route 894.
	Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4), the Commission must consider community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers.
		1.	Community Values
	The Commission has interpreted “community values” as a “shared appreciation of an area or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community.” 
	Links J6, K41, and J33 would disproportionately affect community values.
	Many of the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group properties have been in their respective families for more than 100 years. With this historical ownership also comes a history of stewardship of the land, taking care to preserve and protect their traditional way of life, including farming and ranching on their property.
	Landowners affected by Links J6, K41, and J33, and others generally residing in the southern portion of the study area, share a common appreciation of both the land itself and stewardship over said lands. Farming and ranching in this area is more than an occupation; it is a way of life, passed down by generation after generation.
	Other ranches in the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group are the dreamed-for results of a long and arduous journey. Thomas and Kerrie Heck, owners of Zentonia Ranch, for example, spent their lives working towards one day owning and operating a ranch. Similarly, Royce and Angie Giada have invested both money and hours of hard work in turning a plot of land into a utopia for their family and friends.
	Selecting Links J6, K41, or J33 could jeopardize these ways of life, fragmenting the land and potentially precluding these landowners from sharing in their ancestral or dreamed-for occupations. As such, it is critical that the Commission avoid introducing a new transmission corridor through both multigenerational working ranches and new operations that are the result of hard work, such as these, to avoid severely undermining the shared values in the communities affected by these links. 
	Further, in his direct testimony, Matt Hillis addresses specific community issues regarding the town of Pontotoc that the Commission should consider, stating that the “town has endured more than its share of hardship. A severe typhoid fever epidemic in 1887 nearly wiped out the population, leading to the construction of a second cemetery in 1888. Later, in 1947, a devastating fire destroyed much of the downtown area. These events are not just history; they are part of the resilience and identity of this community. Given this past, it’s hard to justify placing a large-scale transmission line directly through the heart of a town that has worked so hard to rebuild and preserve its character. Pontotoc is still striving to recover, grow, and honor its heritage. Infrastructure decisions like this should reflect and respect that effort, not undermine it.” The rest of the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group echoes these concerns and implores the Commission to reject any route using Link J6, K41, or J33, thereby protecting these communities.
	Route 894 best addresses community values.
	One way to evaluate community values is by addressing the issues raised by the communities themselves. At the three public meetings, Joint Applicants solicited comments and questions from landowners, which they provided in the EA. The community’s concerns included proximity to residences, impact on ranching activities, aesthetics, environmental concerns, and historical resources. As discussed in the Initial Brief and reiterated here, Route 894, in large part, addresses these issues.
	First, only two routes in this entire proceeding affect fewer habitable structures than Route 894. Accordingly, Route 894 protects such structures better than any other viable routing option. Second, Route 894 crosses only 162.8 miles of rangeland pasture, despite it being the most prevalent terrain in these proceedings. Routes 572 and CCG, respectively, cross 6 and 10 more miles of this terrain, meaning 6 to 10 more miles of ranching activities would be deeply affected if either of those routes were selected. Third, Route 894 protects the aesthetics of the area by utilizing the J22 Colorado River crossing, which is outside of the one-half-mile distance, referred to as viewshed in the environmental assessment criteria of the state parks in the area. Fourth, by avoiding Link J31, Route 894 avoids the only known area of golden-cheek warbler habitat. Fifth, selecting Route 894 would best protect historical resources as it is tied for the least number of cultural sites within 1000 feet of its centerline at only twelve, all while avoiding the historic, recognized Taylor-Rose Ranch on Link G6. Finally, meeting multiple key criteria factors, Route 894 avoids the only known school in the study area, the Florence Independent School District elementary school. 	
When focusing on the community’s primary concerns, Route 894 demonstrates it is the least harmful route as well as the route that best meets the statutory criteria.
		2.	Recreational and Park Areas
	The avoidance of recreational and park areas is of vital importance to the Commission’s determination of its best-meets route.
Route 894 does not affect any recreational and park areas, nor the viewshed of the same.
	The avoidance of recreational and park areas is of vital importance to the Commission’s determination of its best-meets route.
	There are two state parks within the study area: the Colorado Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park. Critically, Route 894 has no length crossing recreational and park areas. Further, Route 894 does not have any parks or recreational areas within 1,000 feet of the centerline, nor any length identified by Joint Applicants as being within one-half mile, which is their metric for determining whether the length would be in the visual foreground of any park or recreational area. 
		3.	Historical and Aesthetic Values
	Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), the Commission must consider the historical and aesthetic values and the impact of certain transmission line routes on the community. 

Multigenerational ranches and historical sites on Links J6 and K41 should be avoided.
The historical significance of the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group properties illustrates with particular clarity the factors that the Commission must consider in its historical values analysis.
	Many of these ranches date back to the 1850’s. The Kuykendall Ranch, currently owned by Lisa Kuykendall Whittlesey and her brother, Jeff, was founded by their great-great-grandfather, W.J. Kuykendall, in 1859, running cattle on the open range for years until the land was finally deeded to him shortly after Texas rejoined the Union after the Civil War. Lisa and Jeff are the fifth generation to run the ranch and have continued their family’s historical stewardship and protection of the land, which was designated as a Texas Family Land Heritage Century Ranch by the Texas Department of Agriculture in 2006.
	The Cook Ranch and the Clark Ranch share in this same historical founding, as they were also a part of the original Kuykendall Ranch before being inherited and divided by the children and grandchildren of W.J. Kuykendall. 
Further, the Cook Ranch includes additional sites of historical significance, including the Council Ground Trail. In 1847, German settlers in what later became Fredericksburg signed a treaty with the Penatuhkah Comanche at a site near San Saba, one of the few treaties in Texas history that was never broken. The Cook Ranch holds part of the Council Ground Trail, the historical trail used by the Comanche to travel to this site, on its property, which, according to family history, is marked by a marker tree that has branches pointing parallel to the trail.
	The Commission has historically treated heritage ranches as a historical resource. In his direct testimony and during cross-examination, former PUC Chairman Barry Smitherman reaffirmed this treatment, stating that where there is careful and continuous stewardship of land that is and/or will be part of multi-generational family legacies, the Commission should seek to avoid disturbing the same. There are no better examples of multigenerational family ranches in these proceedings than those on Links J6 and K41; accordingly, in line with the opinion of the former PUC Chairman, these ranches should be avoided, and Links J6, K41, and J33 should not be considered as viable options for this transmission line.
The archaeological sites on Links J6 and K41 should be avoided.
	It was largely undisputed that any route selected by the Commission would impact Native American cultural sites, both known and unknown, recorded and unrecorded. As such, the known sites deserve special consideration in order to minimize the effects that this transmission line would have on precious, sensitive cultural resources. The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group implores the Commission to give great weight to the known sites and take careful steps to avoid them if possible.
	A large number of the above-mentioned sites are present on Links J6 and K41. Archaeologist Mark Willis conducted an on-site review of the same and determined that these sites warrant avoidance. 
More specifically, on the Link J6 site, Mr. Willis identified approximately six features of historical significance. Several of these were substantial, measuring roughly 10 to 12 meters in diameter and approximately 1 to 1.5 meters in height, with all remaining intact. Importantly, the site is in a favorable setting near a spring. In Central Texas, such features are often part of larger prehistoric campsite areas rather than isolated features. A site with multiple large, intact features near a reliable water source has strong potential to contain intact buried cultural deposits. Those deposits may preserve information about prehistoric cooking practices, plant processing, settlement patterns, and repeated use of the landscape. Based on his field observations, Mr. Willis determined that the location on J6 appears to be archaeologically sensitive, believing that the observed features may represent only part of a larger site area, and archaeological deposits may extend beyond the surface. For that reason, ground disturbance near these features could affect deposits that are not currently visible at the surface 
On Link K41, Mr. Willis reviewed a site initially noted and recorded by renowned archaeologist Harry Schafer, which was recognized by the Joint Applicants in their Environmental Assessment as being intersected by Link K41. In his professional opinion, the K41 site is a highly sensitive archaeological location. The size of the site, the number and scale of the features, the previous site record, the apparent integrity of many of the features, and the setting near a spring all suggest a high potential for intact archaeological deposits. 
In light of Mr. Willis’s observations and the necessity of preserving these cultural sites, the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group believes these sites must be avoided, and any route that utilizes Links J6 or K41 should be rejected.
Route 894 minimizes the effects on historical resources.
	Regarding historical resources, Route 894 is among the best-performing routes. Route 894 has only 12 cultural resource sites within 1000 feet of its centerline, tied for the lowest number of any filed route. Similarly, Route 894 actually crosses only two cultural resource sites, which is less than the median of three sites and substantially less than the route crossing the most sites, which crosses twenty. As such, very few routes perform better when considering this criterion. 
Routes 296, 572, and CCG bisect a recognized historical site.
	Routes 296, 572, and CCG all utilize Link G6, which was the subject of several different cross-examination questions. Link G6 crosses the Joppa 1886 Trust property, which, importantly, is a recognized historical site, identified by a trinomial and registered with the Texas Historic Commission. In addition to affecting the unrecorded sites in Link J6, the above-mentioned routes would bisect a recognized historical landmark, a devastating effect on something that should be protected and preserved. Accordingly, Link G6 and the routes utilizing it should be rejected by the ALJs and the Commission.
Route 894 performs favorably on Objective Aesthetics Metrics.
In relation to measuring the aesthetic value under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), the PUC remarked, "[a]esthetic impacts to visual resources exist when the right-of-way, lines and/or structures of a transmission line system create an intrusion into, or substantially alter, the character of the existing view." In determining this impact, the PUC advises, "[t]he significance of the impact is directly related to the quality of the view in natural scenic areas, [and] the importance of the existing setting in the use and enjoyment of an area. 
	Joint Applicants' Data Table confirms that Route 894 performs well on the primary aesthetic metrics. For example, Route 894 has approximately 18.52 miles of right-of-way within the foreground visual zone of Interstate, U. S., and State highways, which is the median for all the filed routes. Further, as calculated by Joint Applicants through evaluation of the length within a half mile of the park or recreational area, a method that is consistent with prior dockets, Route 894 has no length within the defined foreground visual zone of parks and recreational areas with respect to Post Oak Ridge and Colorado Bend State Parks. 
	Joint Applicants’ viewshed analysis methodology is well-established.
	Several parties assert that Link J22 is within the viewshed of the Colorado Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park; however, this assertion conflicts with the Joint Applicants’ determination, arrived at using established methodology that is consistent with the U.S. Forest Service methodology.  The complaining parties are apparently relying on a comment provided to Applicants prior to filing the CNN Application from TPWD. It clearly states that it is a December 2025 draft of an analysis of certain Routes crossing the Colorado River. The Commission can give the "draft," which did not concern the current proposed Routes, whatever weight they think it should be afforded, but after the statutory notice of the filing of the CNN Application by Applicants to TPWD, which included the Routes at issue, it is undisputed that TPWD did not intervene, provide any further comments, nor file any evidence to be considered. Further, there is no evidence in this docket, nor in any others, that the methodology used by the Joint Applicants here has ever been rejected by the Commission.
The Link J31 river crossing would impair the aesthetics of the surrounding area.
In these proceedings, the crossing of the Colorado River was the focus of a significant portion of testimony and cross-examination. It is undisputed by either the Joint Applicants or the PUC Staff witness that the aesthetic values would be affected by any of the proposed river crossings. Accordingly, the Commission must select the river crossing that best minimizes these effects. Crossing the Colorado River using Link J31 does the opposite.
Unlike other proposed crossings, Link J31 roughly parallels the Colorado River for more than 1.5 miles before crossing it. Same is a needless and unnecessary impact on anyone on the river, much less the surrounding properties.  
	Certain parties assert that Link J31 is a superior river crossing, claiming that the existence of a pipeline corridor constitutes a “disturbance.” However, this argument does not survive a common-sense review regarding aesthetic values. Simply, the above-mentioned pipeline corridor is underground, meaning there is little to no visual disturbance. Any arguments to the contrary characterize a strip of native grasses and plant life as a visual disturbance, which is, at best, an exaggeration. Further, the pipeline corridor is over a quarter-mile away from the proposed Link J31.

Utilization of this river crossing would result in the placement of steel-lattice towers on an otherwise pristine and untouched portion of the river and would require clearing a brand-new right of way through a heavily wooded riparian area, substantially altering the existing viewshed.
		4.	Environmental Integrity
The Commission must factor in preserving environmental integrity when deciding where to put the route. 
The use of Links J6, K41, and J33 would affect the area’s environmental integrity.
	The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group properties are a well-preserved and pristine utopia for both wildlife and plant life, containing whitetail deer, blackbuck antelope, wild turkeys, dove, quail, and migratory birds such as sandhill cranes, warblers, hummingbirds, as well as wild hogs, coyotes, and mountain lions, native grasses (such as Little Bluestem, Big Bluestem, and Side-Oats Grama), a large variety of native Texas wildflowers, and other important plant species like the milkweed, which provides nutrients for the monarch butterfly. Further, and likely most importantly, golden-cheek warblers are generally present in the area. 
Additionally, the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group properties, given their unique locations on the border of San Saba and Llano Counties, lie in the watershed of both the San Saba and Llano rivers. 

	Construction of steel lattice transmission line towers could threaten the years of work that the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group has put into their property by destroying native animal habitat and interfering with the natural environment that supports the wildlife on the property, as well as impacting a sensitive watershed. In light of these concerns, the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group requests that the Commission select a route that does not include these links, thereby protecting a historically preserved oasis for wildlife.
	Intervenor Lisa Whittlesey, an experienced horticulturist, also testified as to issues with Link J6 and the effect it would have on the surrounding area. More specifically, the Kuykendall Ranch is a hotspot for monarch butterflies, as it is on their migratory route with significant amounts of milkweed. Maintaining their migratory routes is of the utmost importance, as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service indicates that monarch populations have declined by more than 80% since 1990 and that milkweed is the only plant that monarch caterpillars can eat. Additionally, these plants create critical habitat and are an indicator of broader pollinator health.  Making protection of milkweed even more important, Texas counties along the I-35 highway corridor have growing urban areas and showed declines in spring and fall nectar of 1–5% and milkweed of 4–25%, and milkweed density declined 1–5% across most of Texas. Kuykendall Ranch is home to several native species of milkweed (Asclepias). Because many areas of native habitat are no longer available due to urban growth, transportation/highways, and the clearing of property that destroys natural habitat, avoiding Link J6, and thereby protecting a critical monarch butterfly habitat, is crucial.
The Link J31 river crossing is unfavorable and environmentally destructive.
	Only one party in these proceedings independently and scientifically verified the existence of Golden-Cheek Warbler territory on a Colorado River crossing area, that party being the Colorado River Alliance, located on Link J31. Similarly, Link J31 is the only link in the Colorado River crossing area with a known Golden-Cheek Warbler mitigation bank. 

	The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group does not dispute the fact that each Colorado River crossing is designated as a high-probability area regarding GCW habitat, but there is an important difference between high-probability and certainty. It is likely that utilizing one of the non-J31 river crossings would affect golden-cheek warbler habitat; however, it is certain that utilizing Link J31 would affect golden-cheek habitat. In these proceedings, the Joint Applicants, the ALJs, and the Commission must deal with estimations and probabilities; however, they need not do so here. Rejecting Link J31 would result in avoiding golden-cheek warbler habitat as a certainty. 
Arguments supporting the Link J31 crossing fail
	Two arguments were advanced in favor of the Link J31 river crossing: 1) the “existing disturbance” and 2) Link J31’s purported similarity to a link in a previous docket. Addressing each in turn, both fail.
	The existing disturbance argument was not limited solely to aesthetic values, but similarly lacks evidentiary support as to this factor. The “existing disturbance,” that being the presence of a pipeline corridor in the general vicinity of the Link J31 crossing, is greatly overstated. First, despite the representations of certain parties, Link J31 does not utilize or truly parallel the existing pipeline corridor. Link J31 is more than a quarter of a mile away from the existing corridor. Construction of Link J31 would require clearing a brand-new right-of-way through a wooded area, meaning the existing pipeline corridor would not have any mitigating effect on the environmental integrity of the surrounding area. 
Second, accepting for purposes of this argument that Link J31 does parallel the pipeline corridor, such paralleling is not regarded favorably under the governing criteria or by the Commission, given the requirement for extensive A/C mitigation. In sum, the existence of active pipelines is a factor that weighs against, and does not support, the utilization of Link J31 to cross the Colorado River.
	Mr. Brewer, in his Direct Testimony on behalf of Save the Lampasas, similarly asserted that the Link J31 river crossing is environmentally superior to the other options, likening Link J31 to Link C22 in Docket No. 37448 Gillespie to Newton 345-kV Transmission Line Project. Mr. Brewer also represented to this Court, and in turn, the Commission, that Link C22 was a preferable river crossing in that docket. Assuming arguendo that Link C22 is representative of Link J31, this argument fails.
	In contrast to Mr. Brewer’s representation that Link C22 was preferred, the record, as well as Mr. Brewer himself during his cross-examination, indicated that no approval of any route occurred. The Proposal for Decision in that docket, proffered by then-ALJ Wendy Harvel, who now represents Save the Lampasas, was rejected by the Commission, citing failure of all routes to satisfy the Commission’s statutory and commission rule criteria. As such, Link C22 received no approval from the Commission. Again, accepting arguendo that Link C22 is the equivalent of Link J31, Link J31 should similarly be rejected.
Links U3 and J22 are superior Colorado River crossing sites.
	Out of the six Colorado River crossing sites proposed in these proceedings, two stand above the rest, both qualitatively and quantitatively: Link U3 and Link J22.
	Link U3 is the only river crossing that utilizes an existing, compatible infrastructure corridor, that being an existing transmission line. This crossing offers notable advantages over the Link J31 crossing. First, as discussed above, the pipeline corridor on Link J31 is not considered to be compatible infrastructure. In contrast, here, an existing transmission line is arguably the most compatible infrastructure, given the ability to abut the corridor without the need for A/C mitigation practices. Second, paralleling an above-ground tower structure would avoid additional and unnecessary land fragmentation, whereas paralleling a below-ground pipeline would not offer the same advantage. Third, Link U3 entirely avoids the known Golden-cheek warbler habitat on Link J31. In sum, Link U3 would have the least harmful impact on both the surrounding area and the river itself.
	Link J22 performs similarly. It avoids park and recreational areas and avoids paralleling the Colorado River. Link J31, on the other hand, parallels the Colorado River for over 1.5 miles. While the length of a link in the visual foreground of a river is not a criterion in the Joint Applicants’ data tables, such a criterion should be considered by the ALJs and the Commission in their determination of the best-meets route, given the environmental and aesthetic impacts that visible towers would have on the recreational use of the river. 
B.	Commission Criteria under 16 TAC 25.101(b)(3)(B) compel the selection of Route 894.
	The Commission's routing rule provides that, considering PURA criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line should be routed to reasonably moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise. The Commission also must consider several paralleling factors and whether the routes conform to the policy of prudent avoidance.
1.	Engineering Constraints
The Commission must also consider engineering constraints in the selection of its best-meets route.
Route 894 is constructible.
No party established any engineering constraint rendering Route 894 or any other proposed route infeasible, imprudent, or unconstructible under PURA § 37.056 or 16 TAC § 25.101. The Environmental Assessment reflects that Preliminary Alternative Links were repeatedly refined using updated mapping, stakeholder input, and engineering considerations, resulting in the addition, removal, and modification of links before the Application was filed and ultimately producing 171 Primary Alternative Links. Applicants consistently testified that all proposed routes are feasible and constructible and satisfy the Commission's routing criteria. 

		2.	Costs
	The Public Utility Commission must consider the financial costs of construction when selecting the best-meets routes. When considering construction costs, Route 894’s cost is more than justified by its communal and environmental advantages. 
	Cost contingencies are uniform for all routes.
	Certain parties in their Initial Briefs argue generally that the differences in cost between various routes should be disregarded given the 10% to 15% contingency built into the Joint Applicants’ cost estimations; however, these arguments are implausible, circular, and provide little to aid in the ALJ’s and the Commission’s analysis. More specifically, the Segment K13/K51 Landowners argue that the $74 million cost difference between Route CCG and Route 894 should be ignored, as the 10% to 15% contingency is greater than the difference in cost between said routes, and Route 894 could accordingly end up being more expensive than Route CCG. First, this argument hinges on a generally implausible scenario. Out of Route CCG’s 39 links, 23 of them are also utilized by Route 894. The K13/K51 Landowners’ argument would require each of these shared 23 links to remain the same in cost while the rest of Route 894’s links somehow cause an increase in cost of $74 million, which is both unlikely and unsupported by any evidence presented in this docket. Second, the 10% to 15% cost contingency applies to every route in this proceeding. While it is possible that Route 894 will be more expensive than initially estimated, it is equally possible, if not more so given the unique engineering constraints that Route CCG would involve, that Route CCG would be much more expensive than initially estimated. In light of the uniform application of the cost contingency, this argument is circular and yields little to the ALJ’s and the Commission’s analysis other than an overly complicated hypothetical.
Route 894 is cost-effective.
	The estimated transmission line cost for Route 894 is $1.68 billion, nearly $30 million less than the average route costs of the filed routes in this proceeding. Of the routes less expensive than Route 894, none have fewer habitable structures, none have fewer cultural resource sites within 1,000 feet, none have fewer FM radio towers within 2,000 feet, and only a select few perform better on paralleling, avoiding endangered species, and affecting airports. In sum, given the overall benefits and the relatively low cost, Route 894 is the best meets alternative when considering cost.
	The Segment K13/K51 Landowners cite the 2010 Hereford-to-White Deer 345-kV project as an example of the Commission selecting a more expensive route after a holistic routing analysis, arguing that the same is applicable here and Route CCG should be approved; however, they conveniently ignore habitable structures, as well as other key components of the complex issues in the Hereford to White Deer project. As explained by the Commission:

		3.	Moderation of the Impact on Affected Landowners
Moderation of impact on the affected community and landowners is a critical criterion. The record demonstrates that Links J6, K41, and J33 do little to moderate the impact on the community affected by said links, while Route 894 performs well.
The use of Link J6 could damage the extraordinary cattle operation on the Haverlah Ranches.
Since 2018, the Haverlah Ranch has been a part of various verification programs from IMI Global, Where Food Comes From, Angus Link, and the Global Animal Partnership, which bring a premium on cattle sold due to the policies and procedures that must be maintained on the ranch and with the cattle herd. Further, the Haverlahs log all visitors to the property and have a protocol for truck and trailer washing. Compliance with the criteria for this annual audit requires, among other things, detailed logs of any and all visitors, truck inspections, biosecurity inspections, and training programs for anyone who enters the ranch. 
Should Link J6 or K41 be selected by the Commission, the Haverlah family would face two options: 1) require each and every LCRA and Oncor employee to complete training programs, comply with the truck and equipment washing policies, keep a detailed list of any LCRA/Oncor that set foot on their property, and pray that the construction debris and litter from the site does not affect the biosecurity of their cattle herd, or 2) watch their historical and nationally recognized cattle operation fall by the wayside.
Given the stringent requirements for certification and the incompatibility of construction with these requirements, there is no better example of why the impact of Links J6 and K41 would be devastating to the affected community.
Route 296 would disproportionately impact the Florence community.
	As discussed previously, Route 296, which utilizes Link F34, would directly affect one elementary school and two churches. In moderating the impact on the affected community, avoiding community centers is critical. Over 500 students and countless churchgoers would be affected should any route utilizing Link F34 be selected. As such, this link must be avoided, and any route using Link F34 should be rejected by the ALJs and the Commission.

Potential concerns about future development do not render Route 894 non-viable or subtract from its position as both the clear best-meets route and the least harmful route. Simply, the Commission’s routing rules require evaluation of land uses as they presently exist, not speculative future developments. Further, the Commission can consider what weight to give testimony about such future developments. 
		4.	Paralleling
The Commission prefers to parallel existing infrastructure when possible. With regard to this criterion, Route 894 fares well.
Route 894 performs well with respect to paralleling compatible infrastructure.
	Route 894 parallels existing, compatible rights-of-way (including apparent property boundaries) for approximately 43.9% of its length, including 5.66 miles parallel to existing transmission lines, 4.45 miles parallel to public roads and highways, and 91.75 miles parallel to apparent property boundaries, each of which compares well to other filed routes in this proceeding. 
Alternatively, Route 410 bears consideration. 
	Several parties raised concerns with the weight given to the length paralleling apparent property boundaries, generally pointing out that property boundaries are determined on a tract-by-tract basis using county tax rolls, which do not accurately account for the unaffected tracts that may be a part of the same ranch as the affected tracts. Should the Commission opt to evaluate the routes by ignoring the length paralleling apparent property boundaries and instead focus on the length paralleling existing transmission lines, Route 410 is worth consideration.
	Route 410 parallels existing transmission lines for a greater length than any other route of interest in this proceeding. Route 410 has its flaws; however, if the Commission gives great weight to this factor, as many parties have urged, Route 410 is a strong choice.
		5.	Prudent Avoidance
	Under 16 TAC § 25.101, the Commission must adhere to the policy of prudent avoidance, "limiting exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort." Prudent avoidance requires routing that maximizes distance from habitable structures. Route 894 limits the number of homes exposed to electric and magnetic fields better than nearly every other route filed in these proceedings. Routes 296, 572, and CCG do the opposite.
	Route 894 affects a minimal number of habitable structures.
	Applying the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance to the routes in this proceeding makes clear that Route 894 should be recommended and selected by the ALJs and the Commission. Of the filed routes in the Joint Applicants’ Application, only two routes have fewer habitable structures than Route 894. When considering the lack of added benefits from the routes with more structures, the selection of any route other than Route 894 under the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance would be largely unjustifiable.

Importantly, the Joint Applicants initially identified three structures on Link F34 as commercial/industrial structures. After receiving feedback from the general public, Joint Applicants revised this designation, properly designating one of the structures as an elementary school and the other two as churches. 
	Structures like schools and churches are entitled to great weight when considering prudent avoidance, much greater weight than a typical habitable structure. Given the 500 children that attend Florence Elementary, there is ample reason for doing so. By simply avoiding Link F34, the ALJs and Commission can limit exposure of 500 children and dozens of churchgoers to electric and magnetic fields, an effect that would require eliminating dozens of traditional habitable structures to replicate.

In light of this new information, Mr. Poole acknowledged that Route 296 is not nearly as favorable as he initially believed and withdrew at least some of his support for this route, stating that he would need to reevaluate his decision.

As such, his recommendation of Route 296 was made with incomplete information and excluded data that was material to a proper routing analysis, and the same should be carefully considered in deciding what weight, if any, should be given to this testimony.

These arguments both fail to resolve the issue and ignore the simplest solution: rejecting Route 296.
	First, in arguing that Link F34 can be modified to increase the distance between the transmission line and Florence Elementary School, Save the Lampasas disregards the testimony from their own witness, former PUC Chairman Barry Smitherman, who cited the Commission’s remarks when adopting applicable notice distances regarding habitable structures, stating:

Any suggestion that the commission predetermine the potential impact on a landowner in advance of the hearing is contrary to the due process that is the heart of the CCN requirement.”
	In line with Chairman Smitherman’s testimony, moving Link F34 to be outside the applicable notice distance is not a substitute for an examination of moderating the impacts on the affected community or prudent avoidance. Such a modification ignores the evidence presented showing the harm to the school, students, and the Florence community in favor of a predetermined measure of the impact based upon a 500-foot offset. Examining prudent avoidance and moderating the impacts on the affected community using the evidence presented at the hearing on the merits, one solution would result in no impact on the affected Florence community: rejecting Route 296. The same would also limit the schoolchildren’s exposure to electric and magnetic fields, while not even requiring a reasonable investment of money and effort.

While one then has visions of what such screens would look like (Are they two hundred feet tall? What material are they made of?) and then assuming that placing screens between a habitable structure and powerline is a reasonable, cost-effective method of reducing exposure to electric and magnetic fields, which Save the Lampasas did not establish being engaged in mere speculation, the reality based solution is to simply avoid Link F34.
	The Commission should reject Route 296 and every other route that utilizes Link F34.

VI. CONCLUSION

It better complies with community values, will have a far lesser effect on environmental integrity and recreational and park areas, and fares better when considering cost, paralleling existing infrastructure, as well as complying with the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance.
